entries.name: Volterra n-species conservative biological association system
entries.formula: beta_r * dN_r/dt = (epsilon_r * beta_r + sum_s(a_sr * N_s)) * N_r, with a_rs = -a_sr, a_rr = 0, beta_r > 0
assumptions: n is an integer with n at least 2
N_r is the positive continuous population count of species r

beta_r is a positive species-specific equivalence/weight used to convert population counts into the conserved association value
epsilon_r is the intrinsic per-capita growth or depletion coefficient of species r when interactions are absent
Time is continuous and birth/death and encounter effects are represented as continuous rates

beta_r.meaning: Positive species-specific equivalence/weight in the conserved association value

entries.name: Leslie age-structured population projection matrix
entries.formula: n[t+1] = M*n[t], where M[0,x]=F_x, M[x+1,x]=P_x, and all other entries are zero
entries.canonical_expression: n_next=M*n; M[0,x]=F_x for x=0..m; M[x+1,x]=P_x for x=0..m-1; M[i,j]=0 otherwise
assumptions: Population is represented by female individuals, as in Leslie's original formulation
Age classes are consecutive equal-width intervals and the time step equals one age interval
Age-specific survival and fertility rates remain constant over the projection period
F_x is the number of daughters born in the interval and surviving into age class 0–1 at the next census per female in age class x at the current census
P_x is the probability of surviving from age class x to age class x+1 over one time step
The final age class is terminal and contributes no next age class beyond the modelled life table

n_t.meaning: Column vector of female population counts by age class at census t

M.meaning: Age projection matrix with fertility in the first row and survival on the subdiagonal

F_x.meaning: Daughters alive in age class 0–1 at t+1 per female in age class x at t
F_x.unit: daughters per female per time step

P_x.meaning: Probability of survival from age class x to x+1 over one time step

m.meaning: Index of final age class in the life-table distribution

validity.source_location: Leslie (1945), Biometrika 33(3), pp.183–185; matrix relation on printed p.184, derivation of P_x and F_x on printed pp.184–185
validity.regime: Discrete census projection of a female population with fixed age-specific fertility and survival schedules
limitations: The source's F_x coefficients include survival of daughters to the next census, not merely births during the interval
Leslie notes the fertility coefficients require an approximation based on within-interval mortality and maternal-frequency curves

source_register.title: Verhulst 1838 population-growth law (original French article; accessible English translation)
source_register.use: Scan-based English translation of Verhulst, 'Notice sur la loi que la population suit dans son accroissement', Correspondance mathématique et physique 10 (1838), pp.113–121. Directly states dp/dt = mp - phi(p), with phi(p)=n p^2 as the simplest logistic choice, and gives alternative retardation functions. The equation is directly traceable to the original text through this translation, but logistic growth is already in the Core-15 exclusion registry; retain as primary-source provenance/exclusion evidence, not as a new Core-295 candidate.

source_register.title: Gompertz 1825 original age-dependent mortality law
source_register.use: Original scan of Gompertz, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London 115 (1825), pp.513–583. Article I, section 5, printed p.518 directly states age-dependent mortality intensity a q^x and the corresponding number living L_x = d g^(q^x), with g and q constants and Gompertz explicitly clarifying the nested exponent. Modern mu(x)=alpha exp(beta x) is a reparameterization, not the paper's printed notation. Proposed demographic survival/mortality model; biological-domain scope and structural review remain pending.

source_register.title: Holling 1959 handling-time functional response and model comparison
source_register.use: Original scan of C. S. Holling, The Canadian Entomologist 91(7) (1959), pp.385–398. Equations (1)–(10), printed pp.386–390, derive the handling-time/searching-time response y=T_t a x/(1+abx), including identification-time extension; equations (11)–(13) reproduce and compare K. E. F. Watt's exponential response. Type II rational saturation is structurally equivalent to the Core-15 Michaelis–Menten exclusion and is provenance/exclusion evidence, not a new candidate. Holling explicitly notes the observed S-shaped small-mammal response is not explained by Eq. (4); do not misattribute the later Real Type III model to this paper.

source_register.title: Watt 1959 exponential functional-response model (primary source retrieval lead)
source_register.use: Watt, 'A Mathematical Model for the Effect of Densities of Attacked and Attacking Species on the Number Attacked', The Canadian Entomologist 91(3) (1959), pp.129–144. Holling (1959b), equations (11)–(13), transcribes Watt's model as N_a=P K(1-exp(-a N_0 P^(1-b))) and, at fixed predator density, y=K'(1-exp(-a'x)); the original Watt paper remains access-gated and must be inspected before direct equation transcription or candidate promotion. Additional secondary transcription located in Royama (1971), §4(f), printed pp.56–61: Royama quotes Watt (1959, p.133) as defining N_a, N_0, P, A and K and gives the coupled derivation dN_a/dN_0 = P A(PK−N_a), dA/dP=−βA/P, A=αP^(−β), yielding N_a=PK[1−exp(−αN_0P^(1−β))] (OCR exponent formatting normalized from Royama's reproduced equations). Royama criticizes the derivation/interpretation and distinguishes instantaneous kill count from depletion of prey. This is a secondary transcription only; primary Watt article remains gated and no candidate is counted.

source_register.title: Lotka 1920 original plant–herbivore interaction system
source_register.use: Publisher-hosted full text of A. J. Lotka, 'Analytical Note on Certain Rhythmic Relations in Organic Systems', PNAS 6(7) (1920), pp.410–415. Equations (5)–(10), especially (8) and (10), directly transcribe the coupled plant/herbivore mass dynamics; the author explicitly says A1, A2, B1, B2 are in general functions of both state variables. This is a source-level primary transcription, not a new catalogue equation candidate because the constitutive functions are not specified. The constant-coefficient Lotka–Volterra system is a restriction, not a second independent equation.

source_register.title: Volterra 1926 n-species conservative biological association system (author-expanded 1927 reprint)
source_register.use: Author-expanded reprint of Vito Volterra's 1926 Memorie della R. Accademia Nazionale dei Lincei memoir, with the first three parts rearranged and expanded. Part II, §2, printed pp.38–39, derives the n-species weighted interaction system beta_r dN_r/dt=(epsilon_r beta_r+sum_s a_sr N_s)N_r, with antisymmetric interaction coefficients a_rs=-a_sr, a_rr=0 and beta_r>0. The same source explicitly identifies the two-species feeding model as a special case. Proposed as a distinct n-species conservative-interaction family; compare structurally against Lotka 1920 and all other population-interaction sources before acceptance.

source_register.title: Nicholson and Bailey 1935 discrete-generation host–parasitoid interaction model
source_register.use: Primary publisher record for Nicholson & Bailey, 'The Balance of Animal Populations.—Part I', Proceedings of the Zoological Society of London 105(3) (1935), pp.551–598. The publisher abstract covers random searching, parasite-host interactions, steady states and discontinuous interaction. The PDF and ePDF endpoints are not accessible in this retrieval pass. The familiar discrete-generation pair H_(t+1)=lambda H_t exp(-a P_t), P_(t+1)=H_t[1-exp(-a P_t)] is widely reproduced in later sources but is not transcribed here as a verbatim primary equation until the original paper is inspected. Candidate retrieval lead only; continuous-time Lotka/Volterra systems are not interchangeable with this discrete-generation encounter model. Follow-up retrieval: Wiley/ZSL article landing page exposes bibliographic metadata and first-page image; its Download PDF endpoint returns HTTP 403 to the retrieval service, and direct epdf route is inaccessible. No full-text equations/page transcription obtained. Publisher record remains the primary metadata source. Further primary-source check: Wiley's official article page links an original first-page image (printed p.551), which was retrieved and visually inspected. It confirms the paper's title/authors, receipt date 9 Nov 1934 and read date 2 Apr 1935. The first page explicitly positions the authors' multi-species mass-balance theory against Lotka's equations and says the coefficient functions depend on masses of all species and food materials. This is valuable provenance and model-scope evidence, but it is only p.551; no host-parasitoid recurrence is transcribed from later pages. Wiley PDF remains inaccessible.

source_register.title: Leslie 1945 age-structured population projection matrix
source_register.use: Original scan of P. H. Leslie, 'On the Use of Matrices in Certain Population Mathematics', Biometrika 33(3) (1945), pp.183–212. Printed pp.183–185 define age-specific survival P_x, daughters surviving to age 0–1 F_x, and the lower-Hessenberg Leslie projection matrix M with first-row fertility and subdiagonal survival; n_1=M n_0 and n_t=M^t n_0. Section 2 derives P_x from life-table survivorship and F_x from age-specific maternal frequency with within-interval survival. Proposed as one discrete age-structured population operator, not separate scalar equations for each age class or its eigenvalue/stable-age consequences.

source_register.title: Hassell & Varley (1969), New Inductive Population Model for Insect Parasites and its Bearing on Biological Control
source_register.use: Discrete-generation host–parasitoid model with parasitoid-density-dependent searching efficiency (mutual interference). The commonly reproduced form modifies the Nicholson–Bailey attack term using Q P^(1-m); exact original notation, equations and page location remain unverified because the primary full text is subscription-gated. Source lead only; not equation-ready and not counted as a candidate. Structural caution from Royama (1971), §4(h), pp.66–69: Royama interprets the Hassell–Varley formulation as a special case of a generalized Thompson indiscriminate-parasitism model with a density-dependent hunting coefficient, rather than a wholly separate base mechanism. He writes ln β=ln Q−m ln Y and β=QY^(−m), then combines it with a parasitism encounter law. Treat as potentially same source-family/operator extension; do not count as distinct until original-paper notation and E0–E5 review.

source_register.title: Thompson (1924), La théorie mathématique de l'action des parasites entomophages et le facteur du hasard
source_register.use: Original 1924 French mathematical parasitism paper, Annales de la Faculté des Sciences de Marseille, series 2, vol.2, pp.69–89. Royama (1971) reproduces a Thompson encounter/depletion derivation and distinguishes it mechanistically from Nicholson–Bailey predation; original 1924 scan not yet retrieved. URL points to Royama's secondary full-text comparative transcription, not the 1924 primary article; the primary scan/authoritative landing page remains unlocated.

source_register.title: Royama (1971), A Comparative Study of Models for Predation and Parasitism
source_register.use: Full 91-page secondary comparative synthesis, Population Ecology 13(S1), pp.1–91. Reproduces and critically compares Lotka–Volterra, Nicholson–Bailey, Holling, Ivlev, Watt, Thompson–Stoy and Hassell–Varley model structures. Use for cross-family screening and source leads only; not as substitute for original equation transcription.

source_register.title: Bailey (1931), The Interaction between Hosts and Parasites
source_register.use: Primary journal record, The Quarterly Journal of Mathematics os-2(1), pp.68–77. Publisher exposes title, author and issue metadata plus first-page preview; full PDF is access-gated. A continuous-time host–parasite interaction model lead. Do not infer exact equations from later papers; inspect full text and compare with Lotka–Volterra and Thompson before candidate promotion.

source_register.title: Bailey (1933), On the Interaction between Several Species of Hosts and Parasites
source_register.use: Primary Royal Society paper, Proceedings of the Royal Society A 143, pp.75–88. Royal Society archival referee records from April–June 1933 confirm manuscript title and mathematical review; full article scan not retrieved. Multi-host/multi-parasite coupled-system lead; not a candidate equation until primary text inspected.

source_register.title: Bailey (1933), Non-continuous Interaction between Hosts and Parasites
source_register.use: Primary Cambridge record, Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 29(4), pp.487–491. Abstract says it follows a prior two-species interaction study and establishes fundamental equations; full text access-gated. Discrete/non-continuous interaction lead; do not assume it is merely a time-discretized Lotka–Volterra system without inspecting equations.

fingerprint_scheme.procedure: Parse canonical_expression with the allow-listed AST grammar; declare each variable as a real SymPy Symbol; evaluate the expression; apply sympy.simplify; serialize with sympy.srepr; SHA-256 hash the UTF-8 serialization.
limitations: Variable names are retained, so this hash is not invariant under symbol renaming.
Units and dimensional equivalence are not normalized by this hash.
The hash is a deterministic syntax/normal-form fingerprint, not a proof of mathematical inequivalence or structural distinctness.
Cross-domain analogues, special cases, rearrangements, limits, derivatives, integrals and source-family relationships still require explicit scientific equivalence review.
